backups.overview: Mount Hopper (6,120 ft) is a deep-interior Olympic summit in the Daniel J. Evans Wilderness of Olympic National Park, on the Skokomish–Duckabush divide near First Divide. Its line parent is Mount Steel (6,612 ft), about 1.96 miles west-northwest; Mount Duckabush, Mount LaCrosse, and White Mountain are also nearby. The peak is named for brothers Stanley and Roland Hopper, sons of a Singer Sewing Machine Company executive — Stanley took part in W. G. Steel's 1906 ascent of neighboring Mount Steel. The standard Class 2 line is straightforward climbing, but the historically standard Staircase/North Fork Skokomish approach has been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, and so has the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide that the longer Duckabush River Trail alternative needs, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026.
backups.beta: This is not a technical climb but a serious backcountry scramble: about 13.1 trail miles from the Staircase trailhead to First Divide/Home Sweet Home camp, then off-trail travel east over talus, heather benches, and a short rocky ridge to the summit. Most parties backpack in and camp at Home Sweet Home (just below First Divide) to split the approach over two days. A shorter but steeper off-trail alternative climbs from Lake of the Angels (reached via the Putvin Trail), crossing the ridge and dropping into the valley below Mount Stone before climbing the ridge west of Stone toward Hopper.
backups.turnaround: Given the roughly 14-mile one-way approach and an off-trail final scramble with sparse cairns, set a firm turnaround time on summit day that leaves ample margin to get back through the off-trail section and onto the maintained trail before dark, accounting for possible stream-crossing delays.
backups.comms: No reliable cell coverage along the North Fork Skokomish River Trail or on the summit — this is deep wilderness terrain. A satellite communicator or PLB is strongly recommended given the remoteness and the multi-day nature of most trips.
backups.descent: Reverse the route, descending open slopes and any snow back toward the First Divide / Marmot Lake.
obj_haz: route-finding difficulty (no maintained trail beyond First Divide)

backups.detailed_rack: No technical rack is used on the standard class 2 route — it is unroped scrambling on talus, heather, and a short rocky ridge. Some parties carry an ice axe (and occasionally microspikes) for lingering snow patches on north aspects in June/early July.
pro_tips: Reserve your Olympic NP wilderness permit on recreation.gov as early as possible — summer reservations release mid-April and the Skokomish/Duckabush zones fill quickly.

The Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide is closed along with the Staircase side, so the Duckabush route via Marmot Lake is not an open alternative either; once it reopens, budget roughly double the approach mileage and extra days.
watch_out: The North Fork Skokomish/Staircase approach trail and the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide have been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026 — check the park's trail status before planning either side.
Above Home Sweet Home/First Divide the route is unmarked and off-trail; carry a map/compass or a GPS track.
backups.pro_needs: No technical pro; an ice axe is useful for early-season snow on the approach slopes.
backups.best_season: Late June through early October is the general climbing window, but the most reliably snow-free travel is mid-July through September; First Divide (4,688 ft) and the upper mountain commonly hold snow into July, requiring an ice axe and possibly traction.
backups.approach: The historic Staircase (North Fork Skokomish) approach has been closed since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire, and the Duckabush approach described here is cut too: the Home Sweet Home Trail from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide is also closed, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. The Duckabush approach starts at the Duckabush Trailhead via Duckabush Trail #803. The tread starts easy for about 2.4 miles to Little Hump, then climbs the steep, loose-rock switchbacks of Big Hump before mellowing again to the Olympic National Park boundary around mile 6.2-6.7. Continue up the valley past 5 Mile Camp (a popular fishing/camping flat by the river) and 10 Mile Camp (~mile 12), where the trail's grade eases through old-growth forest along the Duckabush River — reliable water the whole way, though treat it. Beyond 10 Mile Camp the trail steepens again through the rougher upper-valley tread toward the Duckabush Camp junction with the O'Neil Pass/North Fork Skokomish Trail; from there it's a tough, sustained climb — the last mile notably steep — up to Marmot Lake (roughly 20-21 miles from the trailhead), a good base camp near Hart Lake (0.9 mi), Lake LaCrosse (1.4 mi), and O'Neil Pass (1.2 mi). From Marmot Lake, drop back to the Home Sweet Home junction and climb the Home Sweet Home Trail over First Divide (4,688 ft) — closed along with the Staircase side while the Bear Gulch Fire closure stands — then leave maintained trail to angle cross-country/climber's-path up open talus and subalpine meadow toward Mount Hopper's basin below the summit rockwall (high point ~6,120 ft). This upper stretch has real route-finding difficulty: numerous gullies and ribs look equally plausible from below, snow can choke the gully well into summer (ice axe advisable), and the final scramble features loose rock underfoot — expect to backtrack if you pick the wrong line. Given the mileage (~29 miles one-way), most parties treat this as a multi-day trip with a camp at Marmot Lake (or, once its trail reopens, Home Sweet Home) rather than a car-to-car push.
backups.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line: downclimb the same gully/rib system off the summit rockwall back down through the steepest rock step, then the easier talus and heather below it, back to the basin and First Divide (4,688 ft). This is a scramble route with no fixed anchors or bolted stations reported anywhere on it — the standard descent is careful downclimbing, facing in through the steeper rocky steps near the top where the wall lays back into a short climbable face. Some parties uncomfortable reversing that headwall step opt for a single, short rappel off a natural anchor (slung horn or block — bring webbing/cord, since none is fixed in place) to protect the crux; this is optional, not required, so plan on 0 fixed rappels for a typical descent. Watch for loose rock and rockfall onto any party below in the gully system, and re-identify your ascent gully carefully from above — the same routefinding hazard (many similar-looking gullies and ribs) applies in reverse and is arguably worse on the way down. From First Divide, drop back through Home Sweet Home meadow and follow the connector trail down to Marmot Lake, then reverse the Duckabush Trail #803 all the way to the Duckabush Trailhead (an easier but long walk-out, ~29 miles from the high basin). If the historic Staircase approach reopens in the future, the equivalent reversal would instead drop from First Divide down the North Fork Skokomish Trail to Staircase.
backups.bail: Retreat by reversing the route; there is no quick exit from this interior peak.

access.fees: Olympic NP wilderness permit: $8 per adult (16+) per night plus a non-refundable $6 reservation fee (free for 15 and under), or a $45/person Annual Wilderness Pass (reservation fee still applies). Duckabush Trailhead day-use parking requires a Northwest Forest Pass ($5/day or $30/year) or Interagency/Digital Pass.
access.notes: No separate climbing cost-recovery fee like Mount Rainier’s $82 — only the standard entrance fee and wilderness camping permit apply.
access.rules: Bear canisters are required for overnight food storage in this backcountry unit; campfires are prohibited above 3,500 ft; groups are capped at 12 people/8 stock animals within The Brothers Wilderness/Olympic NP on the Duckabush approach; dogs are not permitted once the route enters Olympic National Park.
access.permit: Overnight wilderness camping permit required year-round, reserved via recreation.gov; summer-season (May 15–Oct 15) reservations typically release in mid-April.
access.closures: The road is open, but the approach is not: the North Fork Skokomish Trail from Staircase to First Divide and the Home Sweet Home Trail from First Divide down to the Duckabush River Trail junction have been CLOSED since the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire (20,233 acres, contained 12 Nov 2025) while crews assess hazard trees and repair backcountry infrastructure, with no reopening date on the park's trail-conditions page (updated September 14, 2026) or fire-conditions page (updated September 18, 2026). Flapjack Lakes, Six Ridge, Wagonwheel Lake and First Divide camp are closed as well, so neither the Staircase side nor the Duckabush side has an open trail to First Divide while the closure stands.
access.landManager: Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness) for the peak and upper approach; the Staircase trailhead also lies inside Olympic National Park, while the Duckabush trailhead and lower valley trail are Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District.
access.land_manager: Olympic National Park (Daniel J. Evans Wilderness) for the peak and upper approach; the Staircase trailhead also lies inside Olympic National Park, while the Duckabush trailhead and lower valley trail are Olympic National Forest, Hood Canal Ranger District.
access.parking_pass: Olympic NP entrance fee: $30/vehicle (7-day), $55 annual Olympic NP pass, or $80 America the Beautiful interagency annual pass.
access.passRequired: America the Beautiful / Olympic National Park pass at the Staircase entrance station

overnight_permit.what: Olympic National Park wilderness permit, reserved in advance, per-night fee
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov before the trip; there are no same-day walk-up permits. Bear canisters are required at every wilderness camp in the park, and the Staircase trails are closed after the Bear Gulch Fire, so check status first.

The Duckabush Trailhead (off US-101 near Brinnon) and Duckabush Trail #803 toward Marmot Lake are open, but no open trail runs on from there to First Divide while the closure stands.

climate.fall: Increasingly wet, with early snow possible by October
climate.spring: Wet, with substantial lingering snowpack at and above First Divide into June
climate.summer: Driest, most stable season and the standard climbing/scrambling window
climate.winter: Heavy, wet, maritime snowfall; not a scrambling season and avalanche-prone
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate typical of the interior Olympics: Pacific storm systems drive heavy orographic precipitation, with wet, heavy snowfall accumulating at elevation in winter and often lingering into summer at First Divide and above.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC (Northwest Avalanche Center) — Olympics zone, relevant for early-season snow travel on the approach and summit slopes.

emergency.notes: Because the peak sits near the Mason/Jefferson county line, 911/SAR dispatch routing can depend on which trailhead/side of the mountain a party is on; report your specific location and approach used.
emergency.county: Jefferson County (summit); the Staircase trailhead corridor lies in Mason County
emergency.rangerStation: Olympic National Park Wilderness Information Center, Port Angeles (360-565-3100); Hood Canal Ranger District, Olympic National Forest, for trailhead-specific conditions
emergency.nearestHospital: Mason General Hospital (Mason Health), Shelton, WA — nearest via the Hoodsport/Staircase side; Jefferson Healthcare, Port Townsend, WA — nearest via the Brinnon/Duckabush side

crowds.peakTraffic: If any traffic occurs it's mid-July through August, but even then this is a rarely-climbed, deep-interior objective rather than a trafficked trade route
crowds.estimatePerSeason: Very low — likely well under 20 parties per season; only a handful of trip reports exist online across multiple years

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very high endurance required — long multi-day approach via Staircase/North Fork Skokomish to First Divide or via the Duckabush to Marmot Lake, typically with a high camp before a long summit day
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Overnight/multi-day backpacking load (approx. 30-40+ lb) including bear-resistant food storage for wilderness camping

partner_requirements.approachTime: Typically 2+ days — a long wilderness approach to a high camp near First Divide or Marmot Lake, then a separate summit day
requiredSkills: Off-trail route-finding across broad talus and meadow slopes
Steep snow travel and self-arrest for early-season snow on the approach and upper mountain
Backcountry navigation (map/compass/GPS) in an area far from any trail or quick exit
Wilderness camping logistics and Leave No Trace / bear-canister food storage
Basic Class 2 scrambling on loose rock
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced scramblers/mountaineers comfortable with sustained off-trail route-finding and multi-day wilderness travel far from help; not appropriate for a first scramble given the remoteness and length of the approach.

July.reason: Early July can still hold steep snow; conditions typically firm up into the 'best window' by mid-month as snow gives way to meadow and talus

June.reason: Full snow conditions typically persist on the approach and summit through this period; steep snow travel skills required and route-finding is harder under snow cover

August.reason: Matches the best window — snow has generally receded to meadow/talus travel, most stable conditions of the season

October.reason: Outside the season window; this is a short, storm-prone shoulder season for the area

September.reason: Still within the best-season; stable late-summer conditions but shorter days and rising chance of early storms

weather.typical: Cool maritime interior climate; weather can change quickly far from any trailhead, and this route's long approach means limited fast-bailout options if conditions turn.
weather.probability: Afternoon cloud buildups/thunderstorms are possible July-August; storm risk rises into September.

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Moderate slip/fall exposure — loose talus and meadow slopes plus steep snow (early season) on the upper mountain. Class 2 scrambling itself is not highly exposed, but a slip on steep snow or loose talus this far from help is a serious consequence; the dominant risk factor is the very long, remote approach rather than technical terrain.

avalanche.zone: Olympics (NWAC forecast zone) — NWAC's daily forecast season generally runs winter through spring and does not extend into this route's mid-July–September climbing window

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: N/A - no glacier travel; the route crosses talus, meadow, and seasonal snow slopes rather than glaciated terrain

gaps: Exact Class 2 line/aspect on the final summit block is not confirmed by a detailed published route description.
No confirmed reopening date for the Staircase/North Fork Skokomish trail closure.
No public GPS track found for this route as of this research pass.

approach_variants.name: First Divide from the Duckabush and Marmot Lake
approach_variants.notes: The historic Skokomish approach is closed by fire damage, and so is this one where it leaves the Duckabush: the park lists the Home Sweet Home Trail, from the Duckabush River Trail junction over First Divide, closed for the 2025 Bear Gulch Fire with no reopening date (trail-conditions page updated September 14, 2026), so no open trail reaches First Divide while the closure stands. When it reopens, the way in is the long Duckabush valley over Big Hump to Marmot Lake, then back to the Home Sweet Home junction and over First Divide. Roughly double the old distance and firmly a multi-day trip with a camp at the lake or at Home Sweet Home.
hazards: Loose talus and steep meadow slopes on the upper mountain
Snow choking the summit gully well into summer
Rockfall in the gully system onto anyone below
Burn-scar hazard trees and rockfall along the closed Skokomish corridor
A very long, remote walk-out from anywhere on the route
approach_variants.baseFinding: First Divide is a distinct saddle with Duckabush and Steel to the west and Hopper to the east, and the old climbers' way to the peak splits off here. Do not expect to find it — that tread has been under brush for more than a decade, so treat the saddle itself as the base of the off-trail travel and navigate rather than follow. From the divide, angle east through forest and brush and pop out into open summit meadow, then climb talus toward the rockwall below the top. The identification that actually matters is up there, not at the saddle: several gullies and ribs seam that wall and every one of them looks plausible from the bottom. The one that goes is the line that keeps laying back into short climbable steps; anything that walls up into a blank corner above you is the wrong one, and the honest expectation is that you may back off one and try another. Note a feature at the foot of whichever gully you commit to, because picking it out again from above is harder than finding it from below. The final crest narrows and is impassable in places, so choose your line early.

bivy.name: Home Sweet Home — the meadow camp under First Divide for Steel and Hopper
bivy.notes: THE base camp for the First Divide peaks, sitting in big open meadow about half a mile beyond the divide and roughly 400 ft below it, some 13 to 13.5 miles and 3,800 ft from Staircase. Mount Steel stands about a mile west-northwest of the divide and Mount Hopper about a mile east, so from here both are scrambles rather than expeditions — the two together are commonly done as one long trip of around 32 miles and 4,400 ft total. Hopper can also be taken straight up the slope west from camp instead of using the way trail lower down. This is also the hinge for Mount Duckabush: from the meadow the trail drops north to the Upper Duckabush junction, and the peaks at the head of that valley open up from there. The mileage is the whole story with this camp. It is a two-day walk in for most parties carrying gear, which is why the peaks above it see so little traffic, and why splitting the approach at Camp Pleasant or Nine Stream is the normal way to do it. Wildflowers through July and August, stargazing, and open ground that catches weather — it is exposed, and there is no shelter on the divide itself. Season is roughly mid-July through September; snow holds on the divide and on the north-facing slopes of Steel well into summer.
bivy.water: Reliable through the summer from the headwater creek draining the meadow toward the Duckabush, though the flow drops noticeably by September; fill low rather than at the divide, which has none
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required. This is not one of the named quota camps, so it is far easier to get than Flapjack Lakes, but it still has to be reserved through the federal recreation booking site and it does see demand on fine summer weekends. Bear canisters are required — black bears work this meadow regularly. CAMPFIRES ARE PROHIBITED, well above the 3,500 ft line. Stock is permitted on the valley trail, so expect to share the camp occasionally.
bivy.capacity: A small number of sites spread through open subalpine meadow with a privy; it does not hold large numbers well and the meadow is fragile, so stay on the established pads

bivy.name: Upper Duckabush junction camp — the link between First Divide and the Duckabush head
bivy.notes: This is a connector rather than a destination, and it matters because of where it sits: the point where the trail down from First Divide and Home Sweet Home meets the Duckabush River trail coming up from the east and the O'Neil Pass trail heading west. If you are going for Mount Duckabush from Staircase, you come over First Divide, drop to this junction, and climb again toward Marmot Lake or O'Neil Pass — so the day involves losing about 1,600 ft off the divide and regaining it, which is the reason the peak feels harder than its distance suggests. Camping here is what makes that carry manageable. It is deep valley forest with no views, and it is a long way from anywhere in every direction; treat it as a place to sleep between two big days rather than a base for anything.
bivy.water: Reliable — the Duckabush River at the junction
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, reserved through the federal recreation booking site; not a quota camp and usually available. Bear canisters are required. Below the fire line, so fires are allowed in the established rings outside seasonal bans.
bivy.capacity: A modest forested camp at the trail junction, a few sites; lightly used because almost everyone is passing through

backups.name: Plan 9 from Outer Space
gear: cams to 3 inch (doubles in common sizes)
hazards: Remote, self-rescue-oriented location days from the nearest road, with minimal-to-no cell coverage.
Loose rock on the Barrier crossing and basin-approach traverses.
Exposed simul-climbing required on the summit-ridge descent traverse to the Blob/Terror col.
Seasonal glacier/snowfield moats and crevasses open up on nearby approach terrain as summer progresses into August.
backups.overview: A long, moderate alpine rock line up the right-edge buttress of "The Blob," the rock formation just north of the Himmelhorn in the Southern Pickets, finishing across the exposed "Bela Lugosi Traverse" and up a summit dihedral.
backups.beta: Plan 9 from Outer Space climbs roughly 16 pitches (~1,400 ft) of varied, mostly moderate rock up the right edge of a prominent buttress on "The Blob." The route crosses the exposed-but-moderate "Bela Lugosi Traverse" below a large ledge, then finishes up a steep dihedral of good rock to the summit. The first-ascent party rated the crux 5.10c; a repeat ascent found an easier line and down-rated it to 5.9, and the route is now given a compromise grade of 5.9+ — as with many alpine routes of this style, the felt difficulty depends heavily on which exact line you choose.
backups.turnaround: Given the long, multi-day approach and a remote, self-rescue-only setting far from any road, set a firm turnaround time that leaves ample daylight margin to complete the summit ridge traverse and both rappels, and to be back in camp before afternoon thunderstorms typically build.
backups.rappels: 2 rappels from the summit ridge into the Blob–Terror col notch, then downclimb/scramble back to camp
backups.face: South Buttress of The Blob (aka The Rake)
backups.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (the Terror Basin and Crescent Creek zones are walk-up only, issued in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center the day of or the day before the trip).
backups.comms: Cell coverage in the Southern Pickets is minimal to absent. NPS guidance for North Cascades climbers notes that cell calls from park backcountry, when they connect at all, often route to dispatch centers far from the actual location, delaying response — a satellite communicator is strongly advised rather than relying on phone service.
backups.descent: Traverse the Blob's summit ridge north to the Blob/Terror col, then make 2 rappels from webbing anchors into the notch below.
obj_haz: loose rock (choss) off the described line, typical of Skagit Gneiss in the Pickets
exposed, unprotected Class 3 terrain crossing 'The Barrier' on approach
remote multi-day approach with no quick rescue access
no fixed anchors anywhere on route or descent (aside from old webbing at the col)
weather can close in fast on the long, exposed summit ridge

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
waypoints.note: Standard access point for all Southern Pickets objectives via Hwy 20 near Newhalem; not route-specific beta, but no other approach is documented for this remote buttress.

waypoints.name: Ed Wood Memorial Buttress / Plan 9 from Outer Space start

timing.recommendedStart: Pre-dawn/alpine start from the Crescent Creek Basin camp to allow a full day for the 16-pitch route plus the summit-ridge traverse and col rappels back to camp.

backups.detailed_rack: A standard alpine rock rack up to 3 inches — a single set of cams with doubles in the common finger-to-hand sizes given the route's length — plus a set of stoppers and extra slings for the exposed traverses. There are no fixed anchors on the route itself; the only fixed gear (webbing rap anchors) is on the descent at the Blob/Terror col.
what_to_bring: sturdy approach shoes for talus/slab/snow travel
ice axe for early-season snow crossings on the approach
extra water (basins can run dry late season)
map/compass or GPS for the basin and col route-finding
pro_tips: Go in July while snow still eases travel across the Barrier and basin crossings, before August's glacier moats and loose scree complicate the approach.

The route's grade is famously line-dependent — the first-ascent party rated the crux 5.10c, but a repeat party found an easier line and down-graded it to 5.9, so careful route-finding on the buttress changes the difficulty you'll actually encounter.
watch_out: The "Bela Lugosi Traverse" below the summit dihedral is exposed and unnerving even though it's only moderate in technical difficulty.
The descent ridge traverse to the Blob/Terror col is described by the first ascensionists as "an adventure in itself," requiring short simul-climbing over exposed terrain.
The Barrier crossing on approach is loose, dirty class 3 terrain — a slip here would be serious.
backups.pro_needs: Gear to 3 inches covers the route; no fixed anchors are encountered while climbing (fixed webbing exists only on the descent rappels).
backups.best_season: Late July through September is the usual window. June and early July often still hold more continuous snow that eases travel across the Barrier and basin crossings, but by August Cascade glaciers and snowfields open up with crevasses and moats on nearby approach terrain (noted issues occur around the Otto-Himmel col and Terror Glacier), so timing should be weighed against seasonal melt-out.
backups.approach: From the Goodell Creek group-camp trailhead near Newhalem, walk the overgrown Goodell Creek roadbed for about 4 miles to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing, then climb the Terror Creek climbers' path. The Blob stands above Crescent Creek Basin, so from the Terror Creek side you must cross the Barrier, the loose, brushy ridge dividing the Terror Creek drainage from Crescent Creek; it can be crossed low or high from Terror Basin. Descend into Crescent Creek Basin and camp within reach of the Himmelhorn and the Blob, then scramble to the base of the south buttress. This is a serious multi-day expedition approach requiring a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, off-trail routefinding through brush and talus, and glacier/snow travel gear.
backups.descent_text: From the top, traverse the summit ridge of the Blob northward toward the Blob/Terror col — described by the first-ascent party as "an adventure in itself," with short simul-climbing recommended over the exposed crest. At the col edge, locate webbing rappel anchors over a steep step and make two rappels down into the notch. From the notch, an easy scramble down the col returns climbers to the bench below.
backups.bail: Below the Bela Lugosi Traverse, the moderate, varied lower buttress pitches can generally be reversed/rappelled on gear. Above the traverse, it is generally safer to continue to the summit and use the established rappel-and-scramble descent into the Blob/Terror col than to attempt to reverse the exposed traverse itself.
backups.itinerary: Typically done as part of a multi-day Southern Pickets trip: Day 1, backpack in via the Goodell Creek roadbed and Terror Creek climbers' path to a high camp near the Barrier or in Terror Basin; Day 2, cross the Barrier into Crescent Creek Basin and establish camp within striking distance of the Himmelhorn/Blob area; Day 3, climb Plan 9 from Outer Space and return to camp via the Blob/Terror col rappels; Day 4, hike out.

access.notes: Parkwide about 60% of backcountry sites can be booked in advance, but the cross-country zones this route camps in are not among them: they are walk-up only, issued in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount the day of or the day before.
access.rules: Group size capped at 6 in off-trail cross-country zones (which includes most Picket Range approaches; 12 in on-trail corridors). Bear canisters required in some zones — free loaners at permit offices.

road.name: North Cascades Highway (SR-20) to the Goodell Creek trailhead near Newhalem
road.status: SR-20 is paved to the Goodell Creek campground just west of Newhalem; from there the old Goodell Creek roadbed is walked, followed by a multi-day cross-country approach into the Southern Pickets.
road.driveNote: Roughly 2.5 hours from Seattle via SR-20 to Goodell Creek, just west of Newhalem, followed by a multi-day wilderness approach.
road.seasonalGate: SR-20 closes seasonally (typically mid-fall to spring) for avalanche safety well east of here, near Washington Pass/Rainy Pass (~milepost 134); the Goodell Creek trailhead (~milepost 119, just west of Newhalem) is on the west side of that closure and is not affected by it.

climate.fall: Rock routes reach best condition once snow melts out, but days shorten and early-season snow/storms can return by late September.
climate.spring: Deep, often unstable snowpack; approach terrain remains largely snow-covered.
climate.summer: June-July usually retains more continuous snow, easing basin and col travel; by August, glaciers and snowfields open up with moats and crevasses on approach terrain.
climate.winter: Effectively inaccessible for this route — deep snow, avalanche hazard, and the SR-20 winter closure well below the range.
climate.typical: Wet, maritime North Cascades climate with a heavy winter snowpack and a short, changeable summer climbing window; fast-moving fronts and afternoon thunderstorms occur even in summer.
climate.forecastZone: No dedicated summer point forecast zone confirmed; NWAC's nearest avalanche zone (west-slopes Skagit River area) only issues forecasts mid-November through mid-April, outside this route's climbing season — for live weather, a point forecast for Mount Terror (the range's high point nearest this route) is the closest available proxy.

emergency.notes: NPS warns that cell calls placed from park backcountry often connect to dispatch centers far from the caller's actual location, which can delay response; carry a satellite communicator and plan for self-rescue given the remote, multi-day approach.
emergency.rangerStation: North Cascades NPS Wilderness Information Center, Marblemount, WA — (360) 854-7245; park main line (360) 854-7200
emergency.nearestHospital: United General Hospital, Sedro-Woolley, WA (closest); Skagit Valley Hospital (Level III Emergency Department), Mount Vernon, WA, for higher-level care
emergency.sheriffDispatch: Skagit County Sheriff's Office dispatch: (360) 336-9450 (or 911, which routes to the appropriate agency)

seasonal_guidance.optimalWindow: Late July to mid-August, when the south buttress is dry and snow still eases the Barrier and basin crossings

July.reason: The south buttress dries while continuous snow still smooths the Barrier crossing and basin travel; the Goodell Creek log crossing runs high early in the month.

June.reason: Terror and Crescent Creek basins are still under deep snow with avalanche runout, and the 16-pitch buttress can hold wet ledges.

August.reason: Rock is at its driest, but moats and crevasses open at the head of the Terror Glacier, making the high Barrier crossing harder.

October.reason: Early autumn snow and ice on the loose Barrier ledges and very short days make the multi-day approach committing.

September.reason: Still climbable via the low Barrier ledges, but bare ice and big moats complicate snow crossings and shorter days squeeze a 16-pitch day.

gaps: Difficulty breakdown (physical/technical/exposure/commitment/routefinding) is a computed starting estimate derived from grade, pitch count, and route data on file -- not a researched or crowd-sourced rating. Users can blend in their own read via the UI.

backups.rope_note: No rope length is published for this line, and whatever you carry has to cover the descent as well as the sixteen pitches: the way off the Blob/Terror col is two rappels from webbing, which this route's own hazard list records as the only fixed anchor anywhere on the route or the descent. Everything else you rappel from, you build and leave. The rock is Skagit Gneiss and is loose off the described line.

bivy.name: Terror Basin camp
bivy.notes: The standard base for the south side of the range, and the place the Terror Creek climbers' path is trying to reach. From the flat gravel the basin runs up to a notch on its eastern rim near 6,200 ft, and the Chopping Block, Degenhardt, the Pyramid and the west side of Terror are all workable from here. Whether a party gets this far on day one is genuinely contested — strong parties who know the path do it, and parties who lose the path in the timber routinely do not.
bivy.water: Meltwater off the snowfields above the basin, generally dependable while snow remains and a hunt in a dry late summer. Sources are seasonal, not spring-fed.
bivy.permit: Terror Basin cross-country zone, from Marblemount. 6-person party maximum. It is NOT on the short list of zones reservable in advance, so it is WALK-UP ONLY — up to 24 hours ahead, with permits released in the morning of day one. Fires prohibited; human waste in a cathole, or out in a blue bag above treeline.
bivy.capacity: Small flat gravelly ground for a few tents; the park caps the zone at 6 people per party

bivy.name: Goodell Creek Campground, roadhead staging
bivy.notes: The pavement-level staging camp rather than a mountain camp, and most parties use it to get a few hours of sleep before starting the approach in the dark. Bear boxes, tables and vault toilets mean food and rubbish can be dealt with before you leave the car. Sleeping here advances you toward the peaks not at all, but it does let you hit the roadbed at first light, which matters on an approach this long.
bivy.water: Potable water when the campground is open for the season; the Skagit and Goodell Creek are immediately adjacent as backup
bivy.permit: Frontcountry campground fee only — no wilderness permit needed to sleep here. Reservable through recreation.gov in peak season, first-come outside it; not always open year round, so confirm before counting on it.
bivy.capacity: 19 individual drive-in sites, plus a separate group campground where the old roadbed begins

bivy.name: Old Goodell Creek roadbed near the Terror Creek crossing
bivy.notes: The roughly four miles of overgrown roadbed to the cairn near the Terror Creek crossing is walking rather than climbing, and a party leaving the car late often ends the first day somewhere near here. That is defensible, because the ground above is where the day gets expensive and nobody wants to be finding the path by headlamp. The cost is that the whole climb to the basin still lies ahead, so a low night usually means a full second day of approach with no climbing in it.
bivy.water: Reliable year round from Goodell and Terror Creeks; the last certain running water until the climbers' path regains streams high in the timber
bivy.permit: A wilderness permit is required, and this spot is LEGALLY AWKWARD: cross-country camping in the park is meant to be at least half a mile from a trail and a mile from designated camps, and the old roadbed is a trail. Ask the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center where they will place you before you plan on it.
bivy.capacity: One or two small parties on flat ground beside the old grade

area.name: Mount Fury (East Peak)
area.blurb: East Fury is the more frequently climbed of Mount Fury's two nearly equal summits, sitting at the heart of the Northern Pickets — among the most remote and heavily glaciated terrain in the contiguous US, reached only by a multi-day approach up the Big Beaver and Access Creek drainages from Ross Lake. Elevation has long been disputed: the original 1953 USGS Mount Challenger quad listed West Fury at 8,292 ft and East Fury at 8,288 ft, but a 2019 GPS survey (Eric Gilbertson) put East Fury at 8,322 ft, and a 2022 theodolite survey of both summits found West Fury at 8,305±10 ft and East Fury at 8,356±8 ft — suggesting East Fury may actually be the taller of the two despite West Fury retaining the official 'Mount Fury' name and benchmark. West Fury, reached only via the serious Mongo Ridge or a long 5th-class ridge traverse from East Fury, is rarely climbed and takes a full extra day round trip from an East Fury camp.
